blocks.text: This topic goes deeper into HTTP headers specifically for LLM APIs, beyond the brief mention in the earlier REST APIs topic, covering standard headers, provider-specific custom headers, useful response headers, and important header security considerations.

This topic covers Authorization, Content-Type, and Accept, provider-specific custom headers like organization identifiers, response headers carrying rate limit and request tracking information, and why a secret should always live in a header rather than a URL.
1. Headers as Metadata Alongside the Request

blocks.alt: Headers as Metadata Alongside the Request
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473974303-490983006.png

Headers carry metadata about a request or response separately from the actual body content, information about how to authenticate, what format the body is in, and various other details that shape how the request should actually be processed.
2. The Core Three, Authorization, Content-Type, and Accept

blocks.alt: The Core Three, Authorization, Content-Type, and Accept
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473974303-628106674.png

Authorization carries your API key, proving the request is legitimate, Content-Type tells the server what format your request body is in, almost always JSON for an LLM API, and Accept can specify what format you want the response in, though JSON is nearly universal here as well.
3. Provider-Specific Custom Headers
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473974304-135391235.png

Beyond the standard headers, many providers define their own custom headers, an organization identifier header for accounts managing multiple sub-organizations, or a specific API version header letting you pin to a known version, covered in the earlier API Architecture topic, at the header level rather than in the URL path.

blocks.text: 4. Useful Response Headers
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473974304-209580030.png

This connects directly to rate limiting, covered in an earlier module, response headers often carry genuinely useful operational information, how many requests remain before hitting a rate limit, and a unique request identifier for that specific call, both worth reading and using in your application rather than ignoring.
5. Using a Request ID for Debugging and Support

blocks.alt: Using a Request ID for Debugging and Support
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473974304-761386136.png

This connects directly to prompt debugging, covered in an earlier module, when something goes wrong with a specific API call, having captured and logged that call unique request ID, usually returned as a response header, lets you reference the exact call when reporting an issue to provider support, dramatically speeding up diagnosis compared to describing the problem vaguely.

blocks.title: This is a genuinely practical habit worth building early
blocks.content: Logging the request ID for every API call, even when nothing seems wrong, costs almost nothing and can save significant time later when troubleshooting an issue that only becomes apparent after the fact.

blocks.text: 6. Header Security, What Never Belongs in a URL

blocks.alt: Header Security, What Never Belongs in a URL
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473974304-60916182.png

This connects directly to input validation and prompt security, both covered in earlier modules, an API key or any other secret should always travel in a header, never embedded directly in a URL, URLs frequently get logged by proxies, browsers, and servers along the way, a secret embedded there risks leaking into logs an attacker could later access.
7. Case Sensitivity and Header Naming
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473974305-616998948.png

HTTP header names are generally treated case insensitively by servers, Content-Type and content-type are typically equivalent, though following the conventional casing used in a provider own documentation remains good practice for consistency and readability.
8. A Worked Example Inspecting Real Headers

Inspecting the actual response from a real API call reveals headers beyond just the body content, a rate limit remaining count, a request identifier, and sometimes a specific header indicating which exact API version processed the request, all genuinely useful information an application can log or act on.
9. Headers Set Up the Next Several Topics

This topic sets up the next few topics in this module directly, the request body and response body, covered next, are the actual content headers describe, and status codes, covered after that, work alongside headers to tell an application the complete outcome of a request.
Worked Example

A developer debugging an intermittent API failure initially has no specific information to share with provider support beyond a vague description of when the issue happened, making diagnosis slow and frustrating for everyone involved.

After adding logging that captures the request ID header from every API call, the next time the same issue occurs, they can report the exact request ID to support, who immediately locate the specific failed call in their own logs and diagnose the actual cause within minutes rather than days.
Common Mistakes

items: Embedding an API key or other secret directly in a URL instead of a header
Not logging the request ID header, losing a valuable diagnostic tool for later troubleshooting
Ignoring rate limit information available in response headers, missing an early warning before actually hitting the limit
Assuming a provider-specific custom header is unnecessary without checking the provider own documentation

blocks.text: Practice

Make a real or simulated API call and inspect the full set of response headers returned, identify which ones carry genuinely useful operational information, and consider how you would log or act on each one in a real application.
Key Takeaway

Headers carry essential metadata alongside a request, authentication through Authorization, format information through Content-Type and Accept, and provider-specific custom details, response headers often carry genuinely useful operational information like rate limit status and a request ID worth logging, and a secret should always live in a header, never embedded in a URL.
